entries.source_entry: fact
entries.reason: English fact is an independently productive word base with the modern sense of fact; it descends from Latin factum, ultimately facere. Keep the older make/do sense distinct in the same historical family.

entries.origin: New Latin, feminine plural of Latin -aceus
entries.source_entry: -aceae
entries.reason: An independently documented taxonomic family-name suffix, not the adjectival -aceous already in the dataset. Taber explicitly documents Solanaceae; the botanical code supplies independent formation evidence. This is a scientific family name, with -aceae directly terminal. The related existing -aceous is historically connected, not interchangeable; fungi also use this ending, but the original plant-specific gloss is retained.

entries.source_entry: galvano
entries.reason: A separately attested initial combining form of galvanism, illustrated by the independently defined instrument. Its scope is galvanic current rather than every possible meaning of electricity; original gloss retained with this qualification. No existing exact family identified.

entries.source_entry: nud-
entries.reason: Collins explicitly lists nudi- as a naked/bare initial combining form and cites nudicaul; the other references verify that exact word and its botanical sense. Distinct initial combining form, linked to Latin nudus and existing nud family. Do not reuse nudist, nudity, seminudity, previously related_only on this candidate; the unrelated prior -branch position decision on nudibranch is also preserved.

entries.source_entry: phag-
entries.reason: Independently documented adjective-forming terminal combining form, distinct in function from noun-forming -phage, -phagia and -phagy. The original root gloss eat is retained; the actual suffix denotes feeding on a specified thing.

entries.source_entry: quasi-
entries.reason: Latin quasi has a documented productive initial combining use; quasi-judicial is an independently defined exact hyphenated English example. Means resembling or in some degree; retained as if expresses its historical sense.

entries.origin: Late Latin aeri-, from Latin aer, ultimately Greek aēr
entries.source_entry: aer-
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster explicitly treats aeri- as an air combining form, while Collins verifies the exact aeriferous headword and analyzes it as aeri- plus -ferous. This is a supported position-specific combining form, not an inference from spelling alone; other analyses place the boundary at aer- plus -iferous.

entries.origin: Latin apic-, oblique stem of apex
entries.source_entry: -apec-
entries.reason: The Latin oblique stem apic- is explicitly documented in apical; periapical is independently defined as around the tip of a tooth root and analyzed as peri- plus apical. Thus the cited example places apic medially, while the historical root is not claimed to be a separately productive modern morpheme. Its source companion apec- remains unresolved.

entries.source_entry: -axill-
entries.reason: Medical language source analyzes axill- plus -ary and gives the armpit sense; independently, Collins and American Heritage define subaxillary beneath the armpit, and Collins analyzes sub- plus axillary. Thus axill is medial in this exact sense. Exclude the distinct botanical axil sense.

entries.source_entry: capill-
entries.reason: Historical bound stem capill- is independently documented as hair, and capillaceous is an English adjective meaning hairlike, directly analyzed as Latin capillus + -aceous; it is not simply substring similarity. No related current family was located. An earlier -aceous acceptance concerns the other component, not a negative decision on capill-.

entries.source_entry: cing-, cinct-
entries.reason: University of Vermont lists cing- bind/gird with cingulate, and American Heritage gives English cingulum girdlelike structure, from Latin cingulum and cingere gird. The Latin present stem is a real historical component of cingulum, not an asserted modern free morpheme. Connect the existing cinct bind family g_37a808cb912218b7; the stems are present/participle forms.

entries.source_entry: coel-
entries.reason: Both a medical dictionary and a historical English dictionary define terminal -coele as cavity/chamber, and blastocoele is independently documented as an English spelling for the cavity of a blastula. It belongs with existing coel/-coel family g_c9ea96204b7968c9. Do not conflate Greek koilos cavity with -cele hernia; sarcocele was previously excluded for this cavity sense.

entries.source_entry: cogn/i
entries.reason: The exact historical present stem cognosc- of Latin cognoscere know appears in English cognoscente, which American Heritage documents as an expert, via the Latin present participle. Ohio State Latin grammar independently identifies cognosc- as the present stem. Link cogn/cognit/gnosc family g_84f5ee63e0d9006b only with caution: a prior hold concerns whether shorter cogn alone is an independent morpheme; this proposal accepts the longer historical stem only, without overriding that hold or the related_only judgment for cogn.

entries.source_entry: dec-
entries.reason: Source lists point; restrict to Greek deik- show/point as represented by -deic- in English epideictic, documented by Collins as rhetorical display from Greek epi- + deiknynai show. Klein independently identifies the root and Greek compound; c in English represents k in Greek transliteration. It is not the ten sense from the conflated source card. Latin dic/dict family g_ffcc2de0117817eb is a deeper cognate but has a distinct speak sense; do not merge families without a separate audit.

entries.source_entry: -ty, -ity, -uity, -eity
entries.reason: A word-parts dictionary explicitly records -eity as a noun ending of quality or condition and gives spontaneity; the independent headword defines the exact word as the quality of being spontaneous. Sources analyze the word as spontaneous + -ity or French spontanéité; thus -eity is a surface ending / historical lookup alias, not a claim that the e belongs uniquely to the suffix. Keep it sense-restricted and connect to -ity.

entries.source_entry: flu-, fluv-, flux-
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster explicitly identifies fluvio- as a combining form meaning river, stream, and Collins independently gives fluvio- with example fluvioglacial. The source lists both flow and river; preserve both original strings in source_meaning, but use its exact original sense river as the proposed meaning because flow is not established as the direct meaning of this combining form. The specific adjective relates to erosion or deposition by glacial meltwater. Link the existing flu/fluv/flux flow-river family; the linking o does not stand alone.

entries.source_entry: fod-, foss-
entries.reason: Latin fodio, fodere means dig, and its English derivative fodient is independently defined as fitted for or relating to digging. The Latin present participle fodiens preserves fod-, unlike fossil from the distinct past-participle stem foss-. Link to the published foss- dig family; this is an attested stem with a verified exact-form English derivative.

entries.source_entry: fruct-, frug-
entries.reason: Canadian government language reference explicitly lists fructi- fruit and illustrates fructiferous. Collins defines exact fructiferous as fruit-bearing and derives it from Latin fructifer, fructus plus ferre. Link the current fruct fruit family; the i is the compound linking vowel and this spelling is a valid combining-form lookup, not an assertion of unique segmentation. Prior proposal fixed-b0086 accepted fructiferous only for a separate -iferous scope; no prior rejection of this relation was found.

entries.source_entry: hemo-
entries.reason: American Heritage explicitly records -hemia as a suffix variant of -emia, from Greek haima blood. Salamanca medical dictionary identifies the exact English spelling leucocythemia as a name for leukemia, with the blood element. Keep original source meaning blood and record that the complete ending denotes a blood condition. Link existing hem/hemo/-emia family, preserve -hemia final position, and do not force the h-less word anemia as its example.

entries.source_entry: homal-
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster lists homal-/homalo- for even, flat or equal. Homalographic is independently defined as an equal-area map projection and traced to Greek homalos even plus graphic. The etymological dictionary Origins explicitly relates homalos to homos same, so the existing homo/omal group is historically related, but its current sense one, same is not interchangeable with even/flat. Propose a distinct family for now and retain the related-family reference solely for later sense review; do not merge on spelling similarity.

entries.origin: Latin amicus, altered to imic in Latin inimicus
entries.source_entry: am-, amat-
entries.reason: Latin inimicalis derives from inimicus, from negative in- plus amicus friend; in-imic-al preserves the historical medial imic allomorph. The entire English adjective means hostile or harmful owing to the negation, not friend. The older related_only adjudication p_2959bd9252b008da concerned the distinct nonliteral am/ama/amor family scope, and remains unchanged; no negative decision for -imic- is known.

entries.source_entry: -ist
entries.reason: An independently attested English suffix forming person nouns, borrowed through Spanish; fashionista is a verified English formation from fashion plus -ista. The suffix is narrower than one who in general, typically association or enthusiasm; retain original source gloss. Existing -ist has related history and different form, and the old accepted fashionista relation concerned fashion itself.

entries.source_entry: extrem-
entries.reason: Oxford explicitly records suffix -most meaning the furthest and example topmost; Etymonline independently gives the Old English history. The original source card incorrectly presents a list of whole example words as meanings and labels the group Latin; preserve that raw list separately and use Oxford’s verbatim English gloss as the cited source definition. Do not merge this Germanic suffix with Latin extrem-. Inmost is used because topmost had an unrelated prior exclusion under Greek top place; that exclusion remains unchanged.

entries.source_entry: -pom-
entries.reason: American Heritage independently defines pomegranate and traces it to Old French pome (apple) plus grenate (seeded); Etymonline gives pome apple/fruit, ultimately Latin pomum. The exact initial pom- is part of the historical form pome, and source permits initial pom-. This is a historical component of a common word, not a claim that -e is a separate suffix or that the source also proves embedded -pom-. No prior negative pomegranate relation was found.

entries.origin: Greek skeptesthai, via Latin scepticus and French sceptique
entries.source_entry: scept-, scop-
entries.reason: Common British spelling sceptic has initial scept- and is traced to Greek skeptikos inquisitive, from skeptesthai examine/consider. The original gloss examine describes the historical verbal element, not a claim that a sceptic merely looks at something. English skeptic is the US spelling; link existing skept same-sense family; Greek scop is a historically related viewing form but keep its separate existing family unless independently reconciled.

entries.source_entry: -ster
entries.reason: Collins records -ster as a noun-forming suffix, and Etymonline independently derives the everyday noun gangster from gang + -ster and defines it as a criminal gang member. Prior source-scoped exclusions administer and master are unrelated words whose final letters are not this suffix; they remain excluded and are not used.

entries.source_entry: -holic
entries.reason: Cambridge explicitly treats -oholic as an English suffix variant, while American Heritage analyzes chocoholic as choc(olate) + (alc)oholic. This actual suffix was reanalyzed from alcoholic; alcoholic itself is prior related_only for this source and is not reused. Attach to existing -aholic family; fondness sense is informal and need not imply clinical addiction.

entries.source_entry: Afro
entries.reason: AHD documents Afro- as an initial combining form from Latin Afer, Afr- (African); Collins analyzes Afrocentric as Afro- plus -centric, and AHD defines the exact adjective as focused on Africa or African peoples. This example is suitable for the source gloss relating to Africa and does not reuse the earlier excluded Afro-American or Afro-Caribbean relations. English combining forms written with capitals are not free-standing English word admissions.

entries.origin: New Latin Anglo-, from Latin Angli (the English people)
entries.source_entry: Anglo
entries.reason: AHD documents Anglo- as an initial form meaning England or English; Collins explicitly analyzes Anglophile as Anglo- plus -phile and its noun definition includes an admirer of England or the English. This concrete example supports the original gloss relating to England without broadening it to English-speaking persons generally. The source admits an additional British-culture usage for the whole word, which does not expand the stored prefix gloss. Anglophile was previously accepted under the distinct phil/-phile component, not excluded for Anglo-; earlier Anglo-American, Anglo-Norman, and Anglo-Saxon relations remain excluded and are not reused.

entries.source_entry: Smith, Greek and Latin Roots, Part I – Latin, Chapter 7, §55, table row: mus | mus-culus | muscul-aris | muscular
entries.reason: Independent dictionaries attest muscul- as an English combining form meaning muscle, including the exact common English example muscular. Smith §55 supplies the precise historical chain from Latin mus through musculus and muscularis. Earlier U0031 accepted muscular for adjective suffix -ar and its source-specific treatment is compatible; no exclusion of the standalone word muscular for this sense was found in searched prior proposals. The held phrase muscular dystrophy is a distinct relation and is not used.

entries.source_entry: Smith §55: circus > circ-ulus > circul-aris > circular
entries.reason: Plag, Word-Formation in English, Cambridge University Press, explicitly identifies circul- as an English bound root and cites circular. Smith §55 gives the historical Latin chain circulus > circularis > circular; Dictionary.com independently gives circul(us) circle + Latin -aris and Merriam-Webster confirms the ordinary round-shaped sense. Existing circ has the same Latin circle/ring family and should be linked. Prior circular related_only e_345c4393782aa14306da concerns the distinct circu- candidate as an alleged circum- prefix; that decision expressly derives circular from circulus and is preserved, not reversed. The new Smith source concerns the longer documented root circul-, for which this example is independently supported. Earlier related_only decisions for circulate and circulation under circu- likewise remain unchanged.

entries.source_entry: Peter Smith, Greek and Latin Roots: Part I – Latin, Chapter 11, §77, table row: tabula (“list”) | tabulare, tabulatus | tabulate | tabulation
entries.reason: Smith supplies list for its Latin base tabula; Borror independently lists the root tabul, -a with board, table meaning. Dictionary.com and Etymonline establish the exact English word tabulate and its derivation from Latin tabula plus -ate. The independent word-root dictionary supplies the entry rather than treating a Latin spelling alone as proof. Prior audit/B0235/proposal.json decisions mark tabulate and its derivatives related_only to English table because tabul and table have different spelling; the older source-scoped decision remains intact and is not converted into acceptance for table.

entries.source_entry: Peter Smith, Greek and Latin Roots: Part I – Latin, Chapter 11, §77, table row: situ- (“position”) | situare, situatus | situate | situation
entries.reason: Smith’s source row supplies position and Sheehan independently lists situ- as a base with located among its glosses, citing situation. Dictionary.com gives the precise situ- + -atus historical boundary, while Cambridge and Oxford separately confirm the adjective situated with the spatial sense in ordinary usage, though both mark it formal (Cambridge B1). A0314 judged situated, situate, and situation related_only to the unglossed English sit source because they belong to Latin situs, not Germanic sit; that source-scoped result remains unchanged. Do not include Sheehan’s inherent gloss without an independently verified relevant example; Greek sit food/grain and English sit seated are unrelated homographs.

entries.origin: Greek etymos (true), via etymon (true sense of a word)
entries.source_entry: Smith Greek §110: etym-o-logy
entries.reason: Smith provides the exact etym-o-logy educational segmentation. An independent English stem dictionary explicitly records Etymo true and etymology, while AHD independently verifies the English word and traces it to the Greek true-sense element and -logia. Etymo- is proposed as a position-specific historical combining-form lookup variant of existing etym-, with the connecting o included by convention; it is not a claim about an independently productive present-day prefix. The English word is used in general discussion although its subject is language history. The initial frozen root and 1778 published table do not already contain exact etymo, and the etymology example under the separate existing etym- family is accepted. No same-scope prior negative relation was located.

entries.origin: Greek tithenai (to put, place); thes is a documented English historical/educational root form, within the thesis/synthesis family
entries.source_entry: thes
entries.reason: College Board identifies -thes- as a word root meaning put/place/set in English educational examples; Danner’s separately published English root dictionary explicitly records thes meaning to place, put and includes the exact word synthesize. AHD verifies the normal, general meaning of synthesize as combining elements into a whole. These are specific newly located sources that refute the old blanket absence-of-evidence premise for an English historical/root index; they do not convert the six existing related_only word relations or their source-entry scopes into acceptances. The new supporting word synthesize is not one of those six relations and was checked separately. This source-backed lookup variant is not claimed to be a productive new English prefix or the uniquely minimal Greek morpheme.

entries.meaning: a large-scale or prolonged event or activity of a specified kind
entries.origin: English, extracted and reanalysed from marathon; a variant of -athon
entries.source_entry: Collins English Dictionary: -thon; Merriam-Webster: telethon
entries.reason: Collins independently enters -thon as a noun-forming suffix for a large-scale event of a specified kind and gives telethon directly as an example. Etymonline independently lists -thon as a variant of the marathon-derived form -athon for an extended activity. Merriam-Webster verifies the complete ordinary English headword telethon and its fundraising-program sense, with public news examples. The historical origin as a reinterpreted piece of marathon and the alternative tele- + -athon analysis are explicit, not treated as separate letter-by-letter segmentation. The distinct spelling -thon has no exact current or frozen root entry; it belongs in the existing -athon variant family. No prior negative telethon relation was found in checked data.

entries.origin: Greek phainein, to show or appear; pha- is a historical English word-base index
entries.source_entry: Peter Smith, Greek and Latin Roots: Part II – Greek, §136
entries.reason: The source retains the exact English gloss show, appear, and English word-base references independently identify the shorter pha- as the show/appear element for phase, rather than deriving it by truncating phas or phan merely by spelling. Phase is a common word with a shifted general stage sense; AHD separately supports its astronomy appearance sense. Associate the existing show/appear phas/phan/phen family. The original frozen pha=speak is a separate source-specific sense with a pending specialist example; neither merge, supersede, nor relabel it. The existing phase→phas membership is compatible and no contrary pha→phase decision was found.

entries.origin: English noun light, Old English lēoht / Anglian lēht, from Germanic light/brightness
entries.source_entry: light
entries.reason: An independent linguistics source explicitly analyzes the exact word into two meaning-bearing morphemes. Etymonline verifies the noun light, its Old English history and the historical compound, while Merriam-Webster independently verifies light and daylight senses. The widely understood general-English example satisfies the same documented free-base policy as already published day, air and book. The five older source-scoped delight-family decisions remain unchanged: those words come through French delitier / Latin delectare and are not built from the light morpheme despite later spelling influence. A0156’s general note refers to its three reviewed false relations; it does not establish that the independently evidenced light illumination sense is false. No new edge is claimed for the frozen delight source words.

entries.source_entry: friend
entries.reason: A university morphology teaching text explicitly identifies friend as the free root morpheme of friendship and separately identifies -ship; Etymonline independently gives friend + -ship and traces friend through Old English freond to Germanic forms. This is direct evidence of a distinct free English root in a documented ordinary word, rather than a conclusion based only on attaching an arbitrary suffix. The earlier approved friendship relation for the reconstructed historical fri family and the separate -ship suffix remain unchanged. Friend is a free English root, not a prefix; its historical linkage to fri does not imply that a present-day speaker segments friend as fri + end.

entries.meaning: accept as true; have faith in
entries.source_entry: believe
entries.reason: Two independent linguistics publications explicitly identify believe as a free English root within unbelievable, not merely an inferred substring. The full underlying form loses its silent final e before -able, as the second university text explains; the visible word is un-believ-able. Merriam-Webster verifies the common adjective and its not credible sense, and Etymonline gives Old English belyfan and both source meanings. The existing liev trust family has already accepted believable and unbelievable under a distinct historical scope; no related-only or excluded decision on this example was found. Do not join the homographic liev meaning lift.

entries.source_entry: care
entries.reason: Two independent linguistic teaching sources explicitly identify care as an English root in careful/careless; the first analyzes care + -ful. Merriam-Webster independently verifies the precise ordinary adjective and its attentive-concern sense. The common free noun and verb include the source senses concern and look after. Existing -ful is the other component, not the same family, and unrelated car vehicle/flesh homographs must not be merged.

entries.origin: English sad, from Old English sæd; modern sorrow sense developed historically
entries.source_entry: Oxford University Press, Spelling 2A, Unit 5: Adding the suffix -ly
entries.reason: Oxford University Press explicitly identifies the exact form sad as the root in sadly; Stockholm University linguistic dissertation independently calls sad the root of sadly; Cambridge confirms the exact normal sense and AHD supplies the adjective sense. The frozen engra sad source gives no gloss and all its original examples are saddle-related; its source ID is retained only as frozen-candidate provenance, while source_entry_ids for this independent emotional-sense proposal is empty. The old five related_only decisions and instruction not to associate emotional sad with saddle are retained in full. This distinct independent root and newly sourced sadly do not validate or change any old saddle relation. Existing saddle is an unrelated lexical base and must remain in a separate family.

entries.meaning: forms the past participle of certain irregular verbs
entries.origin: Old English inherited past-participle inflection, a shorter form of the historical -en ending
entries.source_entry: Simon Fraser University, Linguistics 220/222/323, Strong Verbs; Samuel S. Haldeman, Affixes in Their Origin and Application, p. 142, -en participle past
entries.reason: Simon Fraser University lists -n and -en as alternative participial markers for strong verbs and includes know, knew, known. Haldeman independently records historical participial -en and -n and gives blow/blew/blown; Collins or Merriam-Webster separately confirms known is the past participle of know. The ending is a restricted inflection on certain irregular verbs, not a general rule applicable to all English verbs, and does not encode tense by itself. The candidate is the exact shorter written form, not the adjectival -en or causative -en homograph. The frozen -en source and earlier known→know decision remain unchanged. Fixie was used only as a discovery cue; no Fixie text or fields were copied.

entries.origin: English bound form associated historically with Latin volvere, to roll
entries.source_entry: Carstairs-McCarthy, An Introduction to English Morphology: Words and Their Structure (2002), p. 25; California Department of Education, My Vocabulary Connections, Roots – Action Words
entries.reason: The California Department of Education vocabulary table directly indexes the exact form volve with meaning roll, turn and example revolve. An independent academic morphology text identifies -volve as a bound root, including in revolve, and discusses -volu- as an allomorph. Oxford confirms the complete everyday word, present turning sense, and Latin history. The sources support the exact form rather than a spelling fragment inferred only by MorphoLex. Avoid assuming that all words with -volve retain transparent roll meaning; this example is limited to physical rotation. This is a newly sourced orthographic form, not a prior acceptance for the separate spelling -volve.

entries.meaning: forms names of countries or regions
entries.origin: Latin and Greek noun-forming -ia, transmitted in place names
entries.source_entry: morphemes -ia
entries.reason: A peer-reviewed study directly identifies the English country-name ending -ia in two precisely segmented common country names; an independent etymological dictionary records the same element in country names, and a separate dictionary verifies the exact geographical name. Both examples are ordinary geography rather than medical terminology. Retain the source meaning land restricted to country/territory naming; do not automatically import state or medical condition senses from the broader source. The source-scoped exclusions for anglia and danglia remain untouched and neither word is used.

entries.source_entry: John Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 110: hesit (haesit), meaning stick fast, example hesitate. Independently Donald J. Borror, Dictionary of Word Roots and Combining Forms (1960), p. 46, indexes hesit, -a with the same root meaning.
entries.reason: Two independent root dictionaries identify the exact spelling and same English root gloss; the first explicitly supplies the common English example. Merriam-Webster independently verifies the actual modern word sense and Latin origin. The source gloss is a historical sense, and the current word expresses hesitation rather than literal sticking.

entries.origin: Latin vegetus vigorous, vegetare to enliven; English educational/historical form veget
entries.source_entry: Word Information, veget-, vege- (Latin: animating, enlivening; vigorous, active; a quickening action of growing)
entries.reason: Word Information independently supplies the full, exact teaching form and historical gloss, and two independent established dictionaries verify common examples, historical derivation and modern senses. This is a historical indexed stem, not a claim that every derived word literally means enliven. The pedagogic incremental value alongside existing veg is limited but the form and meaning are documented, so recommend acceptance subject to peer review. Word Information has obvious typos in its Latin prose; Latin etymology is supported independently by Merriam-Webster and Etymonline.

entries.origin: Latin -tivus, analogical expansion of adjectival -ivus; transmitted through French and learned English forms; historical analysis of sensitive; alternative modern analyses exist
entries.source_entry: -tive; Oxford Linguistics, Latin Suffixal Derivatives in English, §5.5
entries.reason: Two independent non-MorphoLex sources document the -tive suffix or extended historical form, Oxford traces its exact boundary in sensitive, and a modern dictionary confirms its common modern sense. Frozen original tendency/disposition is retained, while causing and making are not silently asserted for this example. Prior six source-scoped related_only decisions concern different words and per-word boundaries, explicitly acknowledging the historical extension; none concerns sensitive. Preserve all six: notably do not reclassify the t in exhaust, abort- or attent-, and do not replace informative -ative with -tive. Existing -ive and -itive deserve explicit variant links while keeping word-specific segmentation.

entries.origin: French barre, bar; deeper origin disputed
entries.source_entry: John Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 53, Barr
entries.reason: Kennedy explicitly records Barr = a bar and barrier; Oxford etymologist Liberman explicitly identifies English bar- ~ barr- roots and separately identifies barrier as related to bar; Etymonline derives barrier from French barriere < barre. This is a historical/teaching root, not a claim that barrier was formed by adding an English suffix to barr. Kennedy also lists barrel, but scholarly sources regard its association with bar as disputed; do not use barrel as support. Deeper origin before French is uncertain. Older related_only for barri→barrier e_fd85cb74ff44b2473a7f concerns a longer distinct sequence, and is preserved; it is not a rejection of this separately supported barr stem. Prior barri→barricade exclude e_92dc93ddf6220a84bc4a is likewise preserved and barricade is not proposed.

entries.origin: Latin initium, beginning; historically in- + ire, to go
entries.source_entry: John Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 117, Initi
entries.reason: Kennedy and an independent modern literacy curriculum explicitly list initi = beginning; the latter teaches initiate as its example. Etymological dictionaries document Latin initiare and initialis/initium and the stated senses. Treat this as a historically grounded teaching stem, not an assertion that English independently coined initiate by attaching -ate to initi. Previously accepted init→initial e_0494134fa4f069f673c9, init→initiate e_0be72039f6fb266471e3, and init→initiative e_190a652378eb1f54ca59 remain valid for the shorter related variant. The earlier it→initial e_1e85a57be89e450e6289 and it→initiate e_d55baf8d026745b66b53 concern the deeper go stem; no negating in- inference.

entries.origin: Greek histōr knowing or expert, through historia inquiry/account and Latin historia
entries.source_entry: John Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 111, Histor
entries.reason: Kennedy directly indexes Histor = knowing and history; independent Borror lists histor, -i = history. Etymonline traces Greek histōr knowing/expert → historia inquiry/knowledge/account, and Merriam-Webster confirms the current study/record sense. History is common (LexiCore line 571) and the semantic development can be explained without asserting its entire modern meaning equals knowing. Historic- and history are connected, but this proposal does not reassign old source-scoped edges.

entries.origin: Greek horizein to bound, limit, divide; horos boundary
entries.source_entry: John Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 113, Horiz
entries.reason: Kennedy explicitly has Horiz = limit, bound; independent Borror lists horiz = horizon, bound. Etymonline traces horizon to Greek horizein to bound, and MW confirms the modern visible-line meaning. Horizon and horizontal appear in LexiCore at lines 2323 and 3321 respectively. Preserve related_only -on→horizon e_04926cd7c01e6f6acaf8: -on is not an independent English suffix in this borrowing, and this new historically grounded stem does not change that old decision.

entries.origin: Latin mobilis movable, from movere move; historical/teaching base
entries.source_entry: Kennedy 1890, p. 137: Mobil; Membean, mobil, active/quick
entries.reason: Kennedy, Membean, and independent etymological and present-day dictionaries support the complete teaching form, an explicit sense and a common use. Mobility is ordinary general vocabulary; exact mobil- is documented independently rather than inferred from deletion of the silent e alone. This candidate is a longer root index relative to existing mob movement and should not be conflated with the separately published mob = crowd.

entries.origin: Latin opinari think, suppose; historical/teaching stem
entries.source_entry: Kennedy 1890, p. 145, Opin = suppose; Membean opin = think, suppose
entries.reason: Two independent instructional sources, Kennedy and Membean, explicitly document the exact form and sense, and authoritative English dictionaries support the historical source and common example. This is an explanatory historical/teaching stem with a useful meaning, not a claim of productive modern word coinage.

entries.origin: Old French outre beyond, from Latin ultra beyond
entries.source_entry: John Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 146, Outr
entries.reason: Kennedy prints Outr = beyond, outrage. Independent Utah State teaching material labels outr- a variant of ultra- and cites outrageous; Oxford etymologist identifies outr as a historical root in French outrage. Modern outrageous = excessive provides direct useful common meaning. Avoid treating modern anger/indignation noun sense as literally equivalent to beyond. Preserve excluded rag→outrage e_fbc346cac68f6e92a9fc: French outrage was later associated with English out and rage but is not derived from rage; that excluded short sequence is distinct from this independently evidenced outr. Also preserve excluded rag→outrageous e_300ed1c71d4bbd2d5424, which concerns the different unglossed rag source and a false English out + rage analysis; it is not a rejection of independent outr evidence.

entries.origin: Latin succus / sucus, juice or sap
entries.source_entry: Kennedy p.195: Succ — juice; succulent (full of juice). L. succus.
entries.reason: The printed source directly lists the English stem and ordinary adjective; independently Borror, Dictionary of Word Roots and Combining Forms p.98, lists succ and Latin succus as juice, sap. Etymonline and Merriam-Webster verify the historical derivation and actual common juicy-food sense. Kennedy meaning is juice; Borror adds sap but does not change the requested original gloss. Succulent was accepted in the older -ulent relation, not excluded. Preserve the historical boundary rather than implying current English speakers form it productively.

entries.origin: Greek theorein behold, contemplate, theoros spectator; historical/teaching stem
entries.source_entry: Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 205, Theor
entries.reason: Kennedy directly supplies exact spelling and original sense; an independent English morphology instruction identifies theor- as a bound root in theory, and dictionary evidence confirms historical paths and current sense. This is useful for theory/theoretical/theorem as a historical teaching index. The form ends at theor, rather than mistaking initial theo- for god.

entries.origin: French trait past participle of traire draw, from Latin trahere, tractus
entries.source_entry: Kennedy, A Stem Dictionary of the English Language (1890), p. 207, Trait = draw, drawn
entries.reason: Two independent historical educational sources supply the exact trait form with its French draw history and portrait linkage; authoritative dictionaries verify common word, lexical meaning and borrowing. The exact final spelling is attested in portrait, whereas the modern whole word trait means a feature or quality, not generally draw. Distinguish separate trait- in traitor from Latin tradere deliver/betray.

entries.origin: Latin tenere to hold, via continere and continuus
entries.source_entry: 95 Percent Group, Grade 5 Phonics Core, Teacher’s Edition, p.183: tinu, to hold
entries.reason: The independent textbook names the complete four-letter tinu and applies it directly to the very common word continue; independent dictionary/etymology confirm sense and connection to Latin hold. The original BAWF group is a clue, not a separate word-to-root proof or a quoted original gloss. Restrict acceptance to a teaching/lookup form in the hold family, not a guaranteed minimal productive morpheme. Phrase hold together explains remote origin, not an asserted present-day literal meaning.

entries.origin: Latin sancire consecrate; sanctus holy, participial form; English sanctuary through French and Latin sanctuarium
entries.source_entry: Book Bums, Wordology Workshop, Sanctuary, 9 December 2022: sanc = holy
entries.reason: The two independent educational sources explicitly record exact sanc for holy/sacred, and one directly connects it with sanctuary. A dictionary verifies its sacred-place sense and a second dictionary traces sanctus/sancire. Sanctuary is general vocabulary; choose the explicitly specified religious sense, avoiding the modern sanction = penalty sense. Existing sanct→sanctuary e_b8442e9b0a453ee089b3 and sanct→sanctify e_6c008a8c314e0ce41b7d are separate accepted scope and remain unchanged.

entries.source_entry: Kennedy 1890 p.158: Plag = stroke, blow; plague. Borror Dictionary of Word Roots and Combining Forms p.78 independently lists plag, plaga = a blow. BAWF provides group clue only.
entries.reason: The previous Kennedy private proposal kn_2522ac92c7452902 was pending because no second independent source for the exact form was identified. Borror independently supplies precisely plag = blow, resolving that evidence gap; Kennedy supplies the directly matched commonplace word, and dictionaries verify the historical and modern senses. Different sources now support a new root proposal without revising unrelated prior relations.

entries.origin: Latin viscum sticky substance, birdlime; Late Latin viscosus sticky
entries.source_entry: Debenham, The Language of Botany, p. 231, visc(o) to make sticky; Merriam-Webster visc-
entries.reason: Two independent specialist root/word glossaries explicitly give the exact stem; one directly names viscous. Merriam-Webster verifies a nontechnical, semantically matching everyday sense. This is near the general-first cutoff: the BAWF Zipf value 3.1305 is a frequency clue, and viscous is not in local LexiCore 5000. Existing visco→viscosity e_919ae41763773fc16c2a is separately accepted as historical lookup; preserve its note that the o derives from inherited -os- and was not proven an English visco- formation.

entries.origin: Greek kata, through an aspirated variant kath-; in cathedral, historical spelling overlap with hedra initial h
entries.source_entry: cath-
entries.reason: Collins 词典明确 cath- 是 cata- 送气前变体；Affixes.org 独立确认 cath- 与 down；Etymonline 及 Shipley 根词典证实 cathedral 的座位历史和 down + seat。原 cath→catharsis 与 cath→cathartic 都由 Greek katharos “pure”、kathairein “cleanse” 而非此 down 义产生，原来源及这两个旧排除保持不变；cathedral 是另一个根词对，不代表旧例也成立。原 source 还列 back/under/against/degenerative，本建议只采用在引用资料与该例中能核实的 down，不将它们当成 cathedral 的直接义。

entries.origin: English irregular weak-verb inflection, related to the dental past endings; an allomorph of the dental past ending, not an arbitrary final t
entries.source_entry: The Oxford Companion to the English Language, weak-verb classification
entries.reason: Oxford describes the suffix optionally spelled -t and Stanford classifies learnt/burnt as irregular weak pasts with X→Xt. These chosen forms have exact learn+t and burn+t in their spellings, corroborated by Merriam-Webster. Chiefly British learnt and its learned alternative are noted; do not apply this inflection to every verb or infer it from any arbitrary final t. Candidate list left can be past of leave or directional adjective and must not be assigned by spelling alone. Existing -ed past r_fab8c7463613d23a shares the inflectional function; the separate Kaikki rank 5 excrescent -t is not this morpheme. Old lef→left e_d4aa08e09a3c12cf96b8 related_only concerns a different root and directional sense; preserve it.

entries.meaning: making nouns of quality, state, or condition
entries.origin: Middle English and Anglo-French -our, historically related to Latin -or; British/Commonwealth spelling; historical quality/state suffix; distinct from agent -or
entries.source_entry: Online Etymology Dictionary, -or (quality/state sense); Chambers 1908, Prefixes and Suffixes
entries.reason: Etymonline defines quality/state -or and identifies its Middle English -our variant; Chambers independently identifies -our in English abstract nouns. The Oxford study lists favor under Latin verbal noun suffixes, from favere; Etymonline traces favour through French favor to Latin favor from favere, and Merriam-Webster validates the British spelling and goodwill noun sense. Thus favour is a historical suffix-index example, not a claim present-day English invents it by appending -our to fav. A British spelling is essential; US favor lacks exact -our. Do not infer all British -our spellings are morphemes or confuse this abstract-noun suffix with agent -or.

entries.origin: English noun-forming ending associated with -ic adjectives and -ity; authenticity also analyzed as authentic + -ity, with overlapping ic
entries.source_entry: Collins COBUILD, -icity suffix
entries.reason: Collins explicitly calls -icity a suffix that replaces adjective-final -ic and uses authenticity; independently Affixes.org lists -icity as a quality/condition ending and also exemplifies authenticity. Merriam-Webster confirms the current noun sense. Under Collins teaching analysis authentic loses its final -ic before -icity is substituted, i.e. authent + icity; the historical and usual compositional analysis is authentic + -ity (Etymonline). The ic belongs to the adjective in the latter account, so do not count both -ic and -icity as disjoint or claim a unique segmentation. Existing -ity→authenticity is separately valid. Old auth→authenticity e_5a03125cbb27d10a5355 was excluded for wrong author sense and hent→authenticity e_d46b79af45355bb52dcc related_only for a different root; preserve both.

entries.meaning: forms a noun from a verb
entries.origin: English, from historical -our spellings influenced by French and analogy; behaviour formed by analogy; US behavior uses -ior
entries.source_entry: -iour
entries.reason: OED 历史词条明确记 behave 与 -iour 类型形式之类推来源，独立英语构词论文将 behave 与 -iour 分析为名词化，Merriam-Webster 确认行为之义及拼写变体；Century Dictionary 独立将 -iour 记为历史 -our 类型形式，但示例 saviour 表示施事者，不能因此把行为方式义误读成“人”。这是少数遗存词尾、非高产的学习形式；不同派生路径须说明，saviour 的法语借词历史也不同。

entries.meaning: at (a time); toward, in a direction
entries.origin: Old English tō; a historical fused preposition analyzed in some teaching sources as a prefix; time and direction uses share a source
entries.source_entry: to-: Old English temporal and directional uses
entries.reason: Two independently documented senses of the same Old English to form are combined into one root entry so a form is not counted twice. Haldeman lists temporal to- in today, tonight and tomorrow; historical English descriptions give directional to- in together. Etymonline also analyzes these as historical preposition compounds; do not imply productive modern prefixation. Prior day, night and other-component relations remain independent.

entries.origin: English commercial naming suffix, chiefly American; deeper source uncertain; commercial-name function, not a cereal-specific meaning
entries.source_entry: -ola (Online Etymology Dictionary)
entries.reason: Etymonline explicitly identifies -ola as a commercial suffix and explains granola with that suffix; Oxford independently gives gran- plus -ola and its modern cereal meaning. Collins independently describes this suffix in commercial names. The same word may validly illustrate multiple distinct root-word relationships. The suggested source of -ola is uncertain, so do not assert a definite Italian or Latin derivation or chronology.

entries.source_entry: Partridge, Origins, -atim
entries.reason: Partridge 的英语词源辞典单列 -atim 并列 verbatim；Dictionary.com 的英语 verbatim 词条直接显示 verbum + -atim，芝加哥大学 Logeion 收录的拉丁词典也独立给相同词界；Merriam-Webster 确认常见英语义。冻结旧 verb→verbatim e_abcc24e9638ff7c11e61 已接受另一根词关系，此处补充不同词素，不覆盖或改变旧关系；同形 tim=时间或恐惧并非此后缀。

entries.source_entry: Hamans, Folia linguistica et litteraria, sequel reanalysis
entries.reason: 语言学论文直接讨论 sequel 的 -quel 重新分析与 prequel 等后续构词；独立荷兰文学词典说明 pre- 与源自 sequel 的 -quel，Merriam-Webster 确认普通影视及文学例词义。不同学者还将 prequel 视为 pre- 与 sequel 的混合/类推，故保留原始混成与后续可分形式两种视角。既有 sequ→sequel e_6d5488e206f35d84f40c 与 seque→sequel e_29e09b5c22b39ca1b50b 的历史跟随义均保持不变；本例是另一个 root→word 关系，词源上的相关不意味着强行改写原记录。

entries.origin: Latin -tura / -ura; historic suffix analysis may overlap a participial stem ending in t; picture also analyzed as pict- + -ure
entries.source_entry: Latin Suffixal Derivatives in English, section 3.9; PBS English spelling lesson
entries.reason: The Oxford academic study explicitly indexes Latin -tura and English -ture as a nominal suffix and cites picture; PBS independently teaches -ture with picture. Historical picture derives from Latin pictura, related to pictus painted; treating -ture as a suffix variant can overlap the t in the separately accepted pict root, and is not the only historical analysis. Old pict→picture e_cc2f56fa4c953d478f4d and -ure→picture e_f5118e082d555be22c3f remain accepted. The proposed meaning describes nominal action or result, not a claim every modern picture means an act. Prior pictur→picture e_ac02eaeabb726d874581 remains related_only for the distinct source form.

entries.origin: English reanalyzed splinter from vacation, used in blends and analogous formations; staycation is also described as a stay + vacation blend
entries.source_entry: Cambridge University Press, Transitional Morphology, excerpt
entries.reason: Cambridge linguistic research explicitly discusses -cation extracted from vacation in staycation and as a form used in later analogical series. Yale linguistic research independently discusses staycation as stay + vacation and its meaning. Record this as an informal modern vacation-related splinter, not the unrelated letters at the end of education or vacation as a historical original suffix. Do not assert a classical -cation root or a unique derivational analysis where the original word is a blend.

entries.origin: Latin -alitas via French -alité or later English formations; compound of -al and -ity; nationality also analyzed as national + -ity
entries.source_entry: NIH National Library of Medicine Lexical Tools derivational suffix list: ality$
entries.reason: NIH explicitly lists -ality with its quoted source gloss and examples; Partridge and the Century Dictionary also record it as a compound suffix, with -al and -ity. A UCLA linguistics dissertation explicitly illustrates nation→nation-ality. Etymonline and Collins give national + -ity, an equally valid finer historical or layered analysis; the two levels are stated rather than presenting an independent indivisible suffix or displacing existing entries. Nationality is common and has a transparent national-membership sense.

entries.origin: English she, attested in Middle English; used as a prefix or first element of a compound
entries.source_entry: Cambridge Advanced Learner’s Dictionary, she- prefix
entries.reason: Cambridge independently lists she- as a prefix meaning female and directly gives she-wolf; Collins independently defines the complete common-language animal term, and Etymonline independently confirms she + wolf. Although the component is also a full English pronoun/noun, the dictionaries explicitly document this combining use; it is not inferred from shee(p), shelf, or shell. Figurative uses of she-wolf and she-devil are separate from the animal example selected. Independent cross-review: Cambridge directly lists she- as a female prefix and she-wolf as its example; Oxford Learners instead calls she a noun in animal compounds, and Etymonline explicitly analyzes she + wolf. Both lexical/compound and prefix descriptions should be retained; the source is not merely a bare free word used with arbitrary affixes. Female wolf is the literal selected sense; there are figurative human uses too. This is ordinary English and has several attestations such as she-bear, although the animal compounds are less frequent than wolf itself.

entries.origin: Greek -astikos, often through Latin -asticus or French -astique; compound -ast + -ic; enthusiastic also historically analyzed from Greek enthusiastēs + -ikos
entries.source_entry: Oxford Companion to the English Language, SUFFIX: forming adjectives
entries.reason: Oxford Companion directly records -astic as an adjective-forming suffix with the exact ordinary example enthusiastic; Partridge independently treats the precise form as an established composite suffix. Merriam-Webster verifies the present meaning and the historically more detailed Greek formation; neither the tastic celebratory libfix nor a false standalone thus root is asserted. Independent cross-review: Oxford Companion directly indexes -astic under adjective-forming suffixes with enthusiastic; an independent historical English grammar identifies -astic as -ast + -ic and names enthusiastic. Partridge separately describes it as a compound suffix. These constitute direct documentary evidence for a larger teaching/combining form. MW gives a more fine-grained Greek derivation, enthusiastēs + -ikos: record both levels and do not assert that the incomplete English-looking base enthusiasi- is a free base, or that enthusiastic historically arose from attaching an independent English suffix to that spelling. Enthusiastic is ordinary common English and means eager or displaying enthusiasm; its earlier inspiration sense is historical.

entries.meaning: state or condition of being, doing
entries.origin: English nominal variant of -ity from Latin -etās; anxiety historically borrowed from Latin via French; anxi + -ety is a teaching analysis, not historical English coinage
entries.source_entry: NSW Department of Education, Stage 3 Spelling Instructional Sequence, pp.57–58
entries.reason: Sufficient independent evidence for -ety as an English educational suffix variant of -ity and anxiety as a common illustrative word. Anxi + -ety is an analysis of the modern written form; do not assert an English historical coinage or productive rule. The existing anxi→anxiety relation was resolved accept and is preserved; a relation from -ety to anxiety is a separate supported relation. Other senses of -ety (kaikki-suffix-00960-sense-01 and -02) remain separately pending.

entries.source_entry: Online Etymology Dictionary, info-; Skidmore College Library guide citing Oxford English Dictionary info- combining form
entries.reason: Etymonline independently identifies info- as a word-forming element abstracted from information; Skidmore Library cites the OED combining-form entry and gives infographic; Dictionary.com independently supplies the exact analysis info(rmation) + graphic and the common word sense. This is a modern clipped form. Do not claim older information, inform or informal were formed from the new info- prefix.

entries.meaning: a person engaged in an occupation or activity
entries.origin: Middle English -iere; variant of -ier/-er, with Old French -ier influence
entries.source_entry: Affixes.org, -ier / -yer; Online Etymology Dictionary, -yer
entries.reason: Affixes.org explicitly lists lawyer and sawyer with -yer, an occupation/person agent variant of -ier; Etymonline independently has a -yer headword and documents lawyer, while Merriam-Webster establishes its ordinary modern profession sense. This is a limited historical allomorph, not a claim that every -yer spelling contains it: player is play + -er, not pla + -yer. Earlier accepted law→lawyer e_d4c5221fbba035c6fd73 is a different root relation and is preserved.

entries.meaning: an expert in a subject of study
entries.origin: Greek -logia plus English -ist; biologist is also analyzed as biology + -ist
entries.source_entry: Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary, -ologist combining form
entries.reason: Oxford explicitly indexes -ologist as a combining form and lists biologist; Teacher Created Materials independently lists the suffix and the same example. Its instructional larger form does not exclude the more fine-grained biology + -ist analysis. Existing bio→biologist and -ist→biologist are retained. Independent cross-check: Collins documents biology to biologist as the change of -ology to -ologist; biology + -ist is a distinct historic and morphological analysis. Surface bi + ologist overlaps the final vowel of existing bio; no nonoverlapping bio + ologist derivation is claimed.

entries.meaning: view; pictorial representation of a specified type of view
entries.origin: Modern English combining form abstracted from landscape; later English combining form distinct from historical -scap in landscape
entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster, A Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes, and Combining Forms, -scape
entries.reason: Cambridge independently labels -scape a suffix and includes cityscape; Affixes.org explicitly describes common active -scape and cityscape; Merriam-Webster’s combining-form dictionary gives the meaning and cityscape as the precise example. This later English combining form is abstracted from landscape; it should not be read into landscape as its historical segmentation. cityscape = city + -scape. Independent cross-check: The Merriam-Webster Unabridged entry archived by USPTO independently treats -scape as a final noun combining form for a specified type of view and directly illustrates cityscape; Mattiello's morphology paper independently treats cityscape specifically as a combining-form construction. This later form was abstracted from landscape, so do not present the latter's historical segmentation as land + the new English -scape. Cityscape is useful ordinary vocabulary, though less basic than city or landscape.

entries.meaning: a person who creates, builds, or repairs something specified
entries.origin: Old English wryhta, worker or maker, historically related to work; historical free noun also used as final compound element
entries.source_entry: Collins English Dictionary, wright² in combination
entries.reason: Collins explicitly identifies wright as a maker or builder chiefly used in combinations and gives playwright and shipwright. Etymonline independently analyzes playwright as play + wright and traces wright to Old English worker; American Heritage also lists both combinations. This is a former free noun still functioning as the final combining element, with actual dictionary evidence for its construction and clear educational value; it is not the verb write. Independent cross-check: Collins, reproduced at Dictionary.com, says wright is a person who creates, builds or repairs and gives playwright and shipwright. An independent Rwanda secondary-school English textbook explicitly calls -wright a suffix and cites playwright and wheelwright. Etymonline identifies play + wright, a maker, and warns against deriving wright from the verb write. Dictionaries also describe wright as an independent historical noun mainly used in compounds: record that alternative compound analysis and the former free-word status; suffix classification follows the teaching source rather than falsely claiming Collins labels it a suffix. Playwright is a common general word with useful spelling and semantic value; other surviving examples often name specialist occupations.

entries.meaning: full of something unpleasant or bad
entries.origin: English combining form from the past participle ridden, with developed affliction sense; figurative combining form also analyzed as a compound
entries.source_entry: Cambridge Advanced Learner’s Dictionary, -ridden
entries.reason: Cambridge labels -ridden a suffix for being full of something unpleasant and gives exact guilt-ridden; Collins independently describes the affliction-forming combining form and gives debt-ridden; Oxford Spanish/PONS explicitly places guilt-ridden under the suffix and confirms its meaning. Preserve the ordinary hyphen and affliction sense; do not analyze the word as literally riding guilt. Independent cross-check: Cambridge labels -ridden a suffix for being full of something unpleasant and directly uses guilt-ridden. The Oxford Spanish Dictionary, hosted by PONS, independently labels the same form a suffix and places guilt-ridden under it. Cambridge's separate Grammar of English analyzes the same word as a compound whose head means ridden with guilt: this is an alternative description of the same visible boundary, and should be recorded rather than claiming that affix analysis is the only analysis. The figurative affliction meaning and hyphenated example are suitable for general learners.

entries.meaning: a hamburger or similar patty sandwich, with the initial element naming a garnish or substitute ingredient
entries.origin: Modern English combining form abstracted from hamburger; modern burger is also a free noun and cheeseburger may be analyzed as a compound
entries.source_entry: Dictionary.com, -burger³ combining form
entries.reason: Dictionary.com gives -burger as a combining form and explicitly lists cheeseburger; Mattiello independently discusses it as a final combining form in cheeseburger and similar compounds. The modern free noun burger also exists, and cheese + burger may be analyzed as a compound; record the cited final combining-form analysis as an alternative, not the only possible modern analysis. Hamburger is the source of the later element and must not be misread as ham + historical -burger. Independent cross-check: Dictionary.com explicitly records -burger as a combining form from hamburger and directly lists cheeseburger; independent morphological research discusses -burger in this precise example. The source of the combining form is reanalysis of hamburger, not an original historical ham + burger derivation. Modern burger also exists independently as a free noun, so cheeseburger may also be described as a cheese + burger compound. Describe -burger as a final combining form, with suffix as the available schema mapping and compound analysis recorded; avoid pretending it is only a conventional bound suffix. The food word is general and familiar.

entries.origin: Latin cellula, little chamber; New Latin combining form; English surface analysis and historical derivation may differ
entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes and Combining Forms, p.12, first cellul- entry
entries.reason: MW has distinct cellul- senses; the selected first entry denotes a biological cell and the separate cellulose entry is not included. Pearson explicitly parses cellular as cellul/o (cell) + -ar (pertaining to), with optional connecting vowel absent in the written example; Biology Online traces the formation to New Latin cellularis and cellula. Common cellular has biological and telecommunications senses; this example is scoped to relating to cells. Existing cell→cellular remains valid. Independent cross-check: Merriam-Webster's p.12 first cellul- entry explicitly gives 'plant or animal cell' as a combining-form meaning; the separate cellul- entry for cellulose must not be merged. Pearson chapter 2 explicitly teaches cellular as cellul/o (cell) + -ar, with no o in the example. This is a medical-teaching analysis; Etymonline separately gives the history from New Latin cellularis, itself from cellula, and not a direct English cell + -ular coinage. The proposed cellular example means pertaining to biological cells, a general biological concept also used in medicine. Mobile-network cellular is a distinct modern sense and should not be presented as proof of the chosen source meaning. Prior scoped outcomes: The proposal's statement that the existing cell→cellular relation remains valid is incomplete. Frozen relation e_1ef95dbd1a1d362efca9 was split by source: s_523418b0ebd7af73e807 accepted for English cell, while s_46c6544928a8805b6059 was related_only because that source lists -cellular, a longer terminal combining form, not internal cell as that listed form. Both outcomes remain unchanged. See evidence-work/pending-resolution/five-rounds-1663/R01W2/work/proposal.json and evidence-work/pending-resolution/b-pending-reaudit-1528/B0006/proposal.json. entries.origin: French nuclé- / New Latin nucleus, ultimately Latin nucleus; English surface analysis and historical derivation may differ

entries.origin: French meteore and Medieval Latin meteorum, ultimately Greek meteōron, thing in the air; modern meteor is a light phenomenon whereas meteorite denotes surviving solid material
entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes and Combining Forms, p.35, meteor- / meteoro- sense 1
entries.reason: The MW Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes and Combining Forms (PDF p.35, first sense) explicitly labels meteor- / meteoro- a combining form and gives meteor as its sense, with meteoroid as a stated example; meteorite is not that entry's listed example. Independent Etymonline explicitly derives meteorite from English meteor + -ite. This confirms the complete meteor spelling and relation without assuming that an ordinary free noun becomes a root merely by accepting a suffix. The root is longer than either Greek historical component and should not be described as an indivisible Greek root. For the familiar Earth example, a meteoroid produces the meteor light phenomenon while entering the atmosphere and any surviving solid material that reaches the ground is a meteorite. NASA explains this for general readers. The IAU technical definition refers to solid natural material surviving the meteor phase, and recognizes the object as a meteorite during the subsequent dark flight before it reaches the ground. Thus meteorite is not a meteor light phenomenon, and 'has reached the ground' should be identified as the usual everyday Earth explanation, not imposed as the only scientific definition. The close connection is causal and historical, not sameness of meaning. Do not merge MW's distinct meteor- weather/climate sense into the chosen astronomical entry. entries.origin: Middle English via Middle French and Late Latin from Greek diabolos; the root may occur inside a longer word

entries.reason: MW explicitly gives diabol- = devil with diabolism, Partridge independently derives English diabolism from diabol- plus -ism, and Collins confirms multiple senses and Greek/Latin background. The term can mean belief or worship, alleged dealings or devilish behavior, depending on context; do not impose an unsupported religious claim. Root is the complete diabol- without a linking o. A Stem Dictionary of the English Language directly lists diabol = devil with diabolical = devilish; Collins traces diabolic through Greek diabolos + -ikos, and records diabolical as variant/extension with senses wicked or devilish. Partridge traces diabolical from diabolic and Latin/Greek ancestors. This validates the complete formative diabol- and historical layers; do not say the entire word was newly made in English from diabol- + -ical. Use the figurative devilishly wicked sense. Original diabolism remains valid.  Checked 1831 has no exact diabol form. It does contain devil r_4ca85f69fadac59f family g_a6c28b2a35be13f8; Partridge explicitly traces English devil to Latin diabolus and Greek diabolos, so connection is attested cognacy/borrowing, not just similar sense. Family merge remains subject to policy and should preserve source meaning. Original frozen scan reports no exact diabol→diabolism; not an exhaustive archive guarantee. Independently checked staging/full-001 relations: no entries for diabolic, diabolical, or diabolism (bounded to that file).  BAWF restricted private frequency clues: diabolical Zipf 3.0164, diabolic 1.8191, diabolism 0.9305; these are rankings, not linguistic proof. Recommend more familiar diabolical as main example with diabolism retained as secondary validated evidence.

entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes, and Combining Forms, mw-page13-line01542
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster directly analyzes the Greek ancestor as chrōmat- + -ikos and defines chromatic's visual-color sense; the Greek stem occurs completely in the English spelling. The MW combining-forms reference separately lists chromat- meaning color/colored and chromatin; the chromatic example supports only the color sense, not the specialist chromatin sense. This is a Greek historical derivation transmitted via Medieval Latin, not proof that the English adjective was coined by direct synchronic suffixation. Etymonline independently confirms the Greek color etymology, although it analyzes through chrōma/chrōmatos rather than explicitly cutting the English form. UT Austin's lexicon independently lists the stem and adjective but does not explicitly state the root-to-word segmentation. The alleged SpellingCity teaching PDF currently redirects to a product landing page and is not independently verifiable at that URL; do not count it as directly accessible evidence. The MW historical derivation is decisive for the exact stem; whether an additional independently accessible teaching source is mandatory remains a policy question. Chromatic is recognizable in art, general education and music, although more specialized than ordinary color; the visual-color meaning is appropriate, and music is not literally visual color. 1832 already has chrom r_88768b2ed9c7cf19 and chroma r_bba51b8d474078da, each listing chromatic, and chromato r_878c4a3ac3edd754; family g_faec5455e0684d16 is appropriate as historical variants. Preserve their relationships and do not imply simultaneous non-overlapping analyses. Proposal reports no exact chromat→chromatic prior scoped disposition; a search found no matching decision in the checked staging/expansion paths, not a proof of exhaustive historical absence. Midland Naturalist, Scientific Names—Form, printed p. 122, explicitly describes Greek chromat- stem, chromat-icos, and resulting English chromatic. Independently corroborates MW exact historical boundary. This is an older historical source; its prescriptive objections to other established Greek-derived formations must not be treated as modern rules. The 27 MB PDF was directly downloadable; statement checked through the web search indexed transcript because the web reader refused its size.

entries.origin: Latin jacio, jacere to throw; jec- is a Latin stem variant in compounds and perfect forms; historical/educational index
entries.source_entry: jec
entries.reason: The two Iowa source records give jec = to throw, to lie, and interject belongs specifically to the throw sense. Iowa math examples are projection/conjecture; Iowa ELA gives interject/subject. Two Iowa documents are one publishing domain, not independent corroboration. Dictionary.com directly analyzes the Latin past participle interjectus as inter- + -jec- + -tus; modern English interject means insert an abrupt comment. The seventh-grade workbook independently displays ROOT -jec- throw directly next to interject. Treat as historical/teaching lookup and do not claim inter + jec + t is productive modern English derivation. University of Texas lists Latin iacio/iacere to throw and iaceo/iacere to lie, including respective jeci and jacui perfects. Thomas Aquinas College calls the latter a related stative form: separate meanings and lexemes do not imply they must be unrelated historically. No evidence here establishes an independent jec lie form or interject with lie sense; retain Iowa lie as unresolved pending. Borror explicitly gives jec liver, which derives from Latin jecur; Lewis & Short support this nominal etymon. This is a separate homograph from the throw verb, not an Iowa sense and not a basis for merging interject or the family. Verified ject→interject e_6ea7d3ecaf60bf6dbc08 accepted for s_21504d4fb61ea9f0f880, s_45ad3ea0fa37931b3a00, s_4afaa6c8ea8827834ab2, s_b824e9b9f7466f7998d6; inter→interject e_d62ec5db92d19c023592 accepted s_b3af3a12e23902c13e1d and s_cc1d32e263dee62dd1df. No exact jec entry in 1836; preserve all previous scoped records. Suggested family g_51383413f065cdc3 is the throw-only jac/ject family. Oxford Learner URL returned HTTP 403 in this check; it is not needed to establish the example because accessible Dictionary.com directly gives both sense and history. Preserve the full source meanings in source_meanings_review and do not silently convert pending lie into a reject.

entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes, and Combining Forms, mw-page29-line03996
entries.reason: Merriam-Webster directly records insecti- meaning insect. Independent Sheehan reverse listing explicitly maps insecti- to insecticide, distinguishing insecto- → insectology; do not rely only on its grouped forward listing. Webster New International separately analyzes insecticide as insecti- + -cide. Collins gives insect + linking i + -cide, an alternative morphological level and not a claim that i belongs simultaneously to both parts. Insecticide is a familiar household and school context; its actual meaning supplies the intended insect sense. No same spelling in 1836 baseline; no exact source-scoped contrary case identified in the checked frozen/quality records. Preserve any unrelated insect or -cide relations; a new family is reasonable absent a demonstrated existing same-etymology family.

entries.origin: Latin from Greek morphōsis; historical/teaching index, not claimed as a productive English affix in the example
entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes, and Combining Forms, mw-page36-line05009
entries.reason: MW explicitly records the exact final combining form -morphosis for development or change of form; its examples cytomorphosis and heteromorphosis are specialist, not metamorphosis. Independently University of Glasgow thesis explicitly describes metamorphosis with Greek morphosis and meta; Norwegian Academy dictionary also gives meta + morphosis for the Greek ancestor. English borrowed the whole word through Latin, and a verb-derived Greek analysis from metamorphoun also exists. The Greek morphosis component in this word is not demonstrated to be a new English suffix added to meta; recommend a historical/teaching lookup with that qualification. Ordinary school biology and figurative transformations provide general educational value. Existing morph r_bd83ced28e85d336 and morpho r_7f323ade0678ffd5 share g_ca38fe64a4af5a12; same etymological family but not interchangeable modern segmentation. Existing accepted e_679e63a75375518d64cb source s_0cacc4be244bc1b6e7b0 and s_5c66eb2f316e8afb28a9 explicitly limits morpho→metamorphosis to historical-family lookup; preserve it and morph e_7eb9d74a6dde2ffe3216 without reclassifying them.

entries.origin: Latin nuntiare, through French, reflected in the English teaching form nounce; teaching lookup spelling
entries.source_entry: nounce
entries.reason: California education vocabulary notebook directly pairs nounce/nunc, declare/announce, pronounce; independent Complete English Spelling and Pronunciation textbook explicitly segments pronounce as pro- + nounce. MW traces the whole word through Anglo-French to Latin pronuntiare and nuntiare; this is an English teaching analysis, not literal Latin nounce or evidence of modern productive prefixation. Pronounce has both speak-a-word and declare-officially senses; both cited sources are clear. In the sole example nounce is word-final, so -nounce- incorrectly communicates a medial-only placement under project conventions. Use -nounce for this example unless a separately verified and permitted internal-position example justifies -nounce-. Verified nounc→pronounce e_9962dd57f81e75a23872 accepted for s_14e0a378414c2e8dd585, s_17145c706c83683d8d18, s_7feab43a5582001e5e16, s_d77ad1cbbd54e1660b22; noun→pronounce e_a7d4e8329880f6c92f85 source s_34912eb325fa87b3faf4 related_only and hold retained. The latter is not evidence for nounce; distinct target and independent direct educational sources. Existing nounc/nunc/nunci have family g_6074a8102510a746; recommendation is coherent. Stored without position marks to avoid inferring exclusive initial, medial, or final position from one example.

entries.origin: Latin lucrum gain or profit, via Latin and French; historical educational stem
entries.source_entry: lucr
entries.reason: Danner thesaurus directly pairs lucr = money, profit with lucrative. MW attests adjective profitable and historical Middle French/Latin lucrativus via lucratus and lucrari from lucrum, not direct evidence of a modern English coinage lucr + -ative. Independent classroom vocabulary list also directly pairs lucr with lucrative. The sole example lucrative has lucr in initial position; proposed -lucr- would indicate internal position. Use lucr- pending a separately supported medial example. No exact published lucr, nor lucr→lucrative in original frozen root list/relations, found. Existing luc light r_438af9f6af4b03f5 is semantically distinct, so do not merge by prefix resemblance. Stored without position marks to avoid inferring exclusive initial, medial, or final position from one example.

entries.origin: Latin maturus ripe, timely; historical educational stem
entries.source_entry: matur
entries.reason: Sheehan directly pairs matur- ripe and maturity. Etymonline supports maturity from Old French maturité and Latin maturitas from maturus ripe/timely; current full-development meaning is a natural historical extension. Do not infer English formed it only by dropping e from mature. The sole example maturity has matur initial, so use matur- rather than medial-only -matur- unless an independently verified permitted internal example is supplied. Checked existing im→immature e_65211e62e545e6bde774 s_2a9f5b2fe995b220935f and pre→premature e_b35a20fa9fb45991772b s_c1d0cb11941e25ab0ed5: distinct root/word/source scopes, preserve. No exact matur root in 1836 baseline or original frozen roots. Stored without position marks to avoid inferring exclusive initial, medial, or final position from one example.
