entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes, and Combining Forms, mw-page56-line07964
entries.reason: MW directly gives -theist a sense for a believer in specified god(s) and lists monotheist. Partridge discusses mono- + theist; Etymonline instead traces the English noun to monotheism + -ist. Their modern teaching and historical descriptions need not represent the same claimed act of coining. The common school religion example expresses belief in one god. Keep existing the(god)→monotheist e_dc583081b482ad956e38 / s_b7646219932c0e4e94a8 acceptance and god family g_9a4a291343707ce9; do not merge homographic the=put/place.

entries.meaning: relating to belief in a god or gods
entries.origin: English adjectival combining form related to -theist and -ic; teaching and historical analyses differ
entries.source_entry: -theistic; Core Knowledge Grade 3 and Merriam-Webster inline combining-form note
entries.reason: MW explicitly marks theistic as an adjective combining form in an inline derivative note following -theist, but prints no independent -theistic sense gloss or example in that note. Core Knowledge Grade 3, printed p.193, explicitly gives -theistic a meaning of relating to a god and links mono- plus -theistic with monotheistic; printed p.52 also pairs it with polytheistic. This supplies a direct independent source for the sense and examples, not merely an inferred gloss and not an MW quotation. Etymonline gives monotheistic ← monotheist + -ic, with monotheist ← monotheism + -ist: document the teaching decomposition alongside, not as proof of direct historical coinage. The proposal meaning field null should be populated for any publication from the attributed Core Knowledge gloss using appropriate permitted wording, rather than inventing an MW source gloss; assess source license before republication. The source’s Middle French etymology expressly concerns -theist, not a separate historical derivation of -theistic; characterize the latter as adjectival relation/analysis, not direct MW origin statement. Same god family as -theism, distinct from unrelated the=place. No exact same-form old negative found in inspected proposal and baseline; do not extend to uninspected historical records.

entries.source_entry: Merriam-Webster Dictionary of Prefixes, Suffixes, and Combining Forms, mw-page54-line07651
entries.reason: MW directly lists strato- meaning stratus and with stratocumulus; an independent Collins entry directly gives the same pairing. Wiley p.14 separately explains strato- in stratocumulus as a low layered cloud and -cumulus as vertical development. School weather context gives educational relevance though individual cloud taxonomy is more specialized than everyday cloud. Same family as strat=layer, not unrelated Greek strat=army. This cloud sense cannot be conflated with the second source’s clipped stratosphere sense.

entries.origin: Latin medicus physician, healing, from mederi to heal
entries.source_entry: medic
entries.reason: Literacy Alberta tutor guide PDF p.173 directly calls medic the root and lists medical and medicine. A separately authored healthcare textbook Appendix C p.552 explicitly analyzes medical as medic + -al with medic = healing. Etymonline traces medical to Middle French médical / Late Latin medicalis and Latin medicus, so preserve the teaching/historical base and do not claim the independent modern English noun medic historically generated the earlier borrowed medical. Medical is a general English adjective used in ordinary healthcare contexts, despite the field association. Existing -ine→medicine e_88548d80c64ae84c36ec, source s_d75d0f9d99ca9f926d7a, is accepted in fixed-b0088 and remains; it does not settle medic→medical. Existing med r_8ea13031bb1d5e41 g_8fc47ee39d1808ec is a distinct middle sense, not a family to merge on spelling alone.

entries.origin: Latin ration-, oblique stem of ratio, reason or reckoning
entries.source_entry: ration
entries.reason: Oxford scholarly book Latin Suffixal Derivatives lists rational under Latin rationalis and explicitly gives ratio/ration- with account/reason; Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary independently identifies ratio(n-) reckoning/reason as the antecedent of rationalis, whose neuter is rationale. Thus ration- is independently supported as the full n-bearing Latin oblique stem / historical lookup, not ration (English food-allotment noun) + al as a historical derivation. English rational carries the common reason sense. The proposal’s family note describes everyday ration as an “unrelated” sense: replace that ambiguous language with “a different modern sense but etymologically related”; Partridge and Etymonline trace ration, rational, and ratio to the same Latin ratio/ration- etymological family. This does not assign today’s ration meaning to rational or establish a direct derivation from the English food word. Existing rat→rational e_be4f06307066aee6348c accepts the three cited source IDs in fixed-b0149; -al→rational e_4f0f5e6ae85b2d99adb9 accepts source s_8cda22170e0e77fdf78d. Preserve both as separately scoped edges. Existing rat r_7877a731b25ec86d, family g_7877a731b25ec86d, also contains ration and ratio as related historical cognates.

entries.origin: English perma(nent), initially in clipped blends and later analyzed as a prefix
entries.source_entry: perma-
entries.reason: Cambridge Guide to English Usage independently lists perma- as a prefix derived from permanent and explicitly lists permafrost; NASA Goddard explains the precise perma + frost teaching boundary. Collins states the original word arose from perma(nent) + frost, and a university linguistics textbook lists it as a blend with later possible affix analysis. Thus retain both the historical clipped compound and modern prefix analysis; avoid implying a previously independent productive prefix had already existed when the source word was coined. NASA defines soil frozen for at least two years, not forever. Permafrost is a broadly useful climate and geography term, though somewhat specialized. For further support Collins analyzes later permacrisis as perma- + crisis. frost→permafrost e_2157538db4d40f8738b0 for s_ca4cb19dcb547a9fcb19 was initially pending in fixed-b0066 and later accepted in imports/resolved-pending.json. Preserve both documented stages, and note this is the frost edge, not an old decision on perma-. Deeper Latin man=stay family relationship is possible ancestry only; avoid automatic family merge based solely on substring.

entries.meaning: misleading image-making or diversion to conceal less favorable conduct
entries.origin: English reanalyzed final element from figurative whitewashing / whitewash
entries.source_entry: -washing; Kramar and Ilchenko 2023
entries.reason: Kramar and Ilchenko (2023), p.19, explicitly call -washing a productive suffix derived from figurative whitewashing and use greenwashing as an example. Cambridge Dictionary has a distinct -washing suffix entry describing organization-level misleading public support and illustrating pinkwashing/bluewashing; this is independent of the journal source. Cambridge has a different -wash suffix used to form verbs: -wash and -washing are related forms but should not be silently collapsed with each other or with free wash. Journal publisher states CC BY 4.0. The journal gives greenwashing directly under this sense; Dictionary.com independently explains the deceptive environmental-image noun and identifies its present form as greenwash + -ing, with greenwash linked to green and (white)wash or (brain)wash. Its lexicographers separately say -washing in greenwashing and sportswashing derives from whitewash. Retain both levels: inherited derivation/analogy and modern reusable ending; do not claim the English word must originally have been formed directly from a previously productive suffix. This is common public environmental vocabulary. Dictionary.com directly defines sportswashing as using sport to mitigate unfavorable reputation or publicity and separately gives sportswash + -ing. Its lexicographic discussion recognizes the -washing element across this and greenwashing. A public policy research report independently distinguishes environmental claims from sport as the medium for reputational distraction. The example supports the general misleading-image sense, but a sport event need not itself assert environmental protection, ethical progress, or an explicit lie. Describe distraction from adverse conduct as the relevant typical usage, without implying that every sports sponsorship is deceptive. Sportswashing is more domain-specific than greenwashing but appears in widely accessible public reporting. 1840 baseline includes free root wash r_48e786955514b9cf g_e14cc5b60f9694e7 with physical cleaning gloss. The source-scoped wash→brainwashing e_ef51f9dc3c46f383a4af / s_2addfb2bf93912bd2e20 was accepted historically as a figurative calque of Chinese 洗腦, not as this whitewash-derived reputational suffix. Preserve it. -washing is historically related to wash through whitewash, but figurative and literal senses, class, and derivational histories are distinct; record relationship without an automatic family merge. No exact greenwashing/sportswashing edge or -washing spelling was found in the checked baseline/frozen records; this is not a claim about all unsearched records.

entries.origin: Latin ferre, to bear, via -fer and -ous
entries.source_entry: -ferous; Collins and Affixes.org
entries.reason: Collins and independent Affixes.org explicitly list -ferous bearing with coniferous. Coniferous means cone-bearing, including in ordinary school nature study. In a teaching analysis coni + -ferous, the i appears before the suffix and may alternatively be grouped in the longer -iferous; historical Latin conifer + -ous and Etymonline’s date show that treating the English noun conifer as necessarily the immediate earlier base is unwarranted. The two analyses have overlapping spans, not two nonoverlapping suffixes in a single parse. Critically, the proposed accepted meaning copies the full Kaikki/Wiktionary source definition verbatim although that CC BY-SA/GFDL source was restricted to discovery. Before release use the independent Collins gloss “bearing”, clearly attribute it, and do not copy the restricted phrase. fer→coniferous e_c28c590325045aac7770 for s_449825312ebe3874f434 was accepted in 263-supported-additions; -iferous→coniferous e_60aa2d1617ab6ba3d00f for s_5cb4315659a034ece7d4 was accepted in 979-supported-additions. Both remain; do not merge fer=carry with any fer=strike. The suggested association with -iferous is a documented form variant, with word-analysis overlap explicit.

entries.meaning: dismissive reference to jargon or confusing talk of a specified kind
entries.origin: English babble, as a final combining form or suffix
entries.source_entry: -babble
entries.reason: Collins dictionaries give colloquial psychological jargon and superficial or confusing psychology-derived talk. Agha 2015 PDF page 9 (printed p.314) explicitly calls -babble a metalinguistic suffix and lists psychobabble; do not suggest neutral psychology writing. Collins combines -babble with this exact example; MW defines technical jargon and states techno- plus the free noun babble. The morphologically free compound and final-combining-form classification coexist; no claim of suffix-only coinage. 1842 has psycho r_57b1c0268510d883 and techno r_a0a925a6a0382247, no exact -babble or listed examples. Preserve existing separate roots. Earlier author checked staging/full-001; no exhaustive claim of no historic conflicts. Merriam-Webster defines technobabble broadly as technical jargon; its explanatory text adds unintelligibility to the listener. Treat negative tone as normal evaluative sense rather than asserting every instance is objectively misleading.

entries.meaning: suitable or easy to use for a specified person or purpose
entries.origin: English adjective friendly, used as a final combining form
entries.source_entry: -friendly
entries.reason: Collins COBUILD public page directly lists -friendly as a combining form; suitability/ease and environmental non-harm are distinct senses. Merriam-Webster gives user-friendly as easy to use/understand; Oxford grammar treats user-friendly as a compound. Accademia discusses final combining use while citing Cambridge and so is not independent evidence of an additional dictionary entry. Dictionary.com provides another accessible full combining-form entry and usage example user-friendly. Accept only suitability/ease-of-use sense with user-friendly. The original proposal meaning string currently includes a second environmental sense despite one example, so remove it from any released/apply meaning or keep it as explicit separate pending sense; preserve original complete Collins entry in private source record. Do not claim user-friendly proves the environmental sense. Confirmed fri→friendly e_979da3bc619144ec1670, source s_6297aa6647c2a92b66c3, originally related_only then accepted as historical family retrieval in A0063; not a modern fri segmentation. -ly→friendly e_b332307d24fb7a63e642 source s_686ec597a412108a8ce2 accepted. Both concern friendly rather than new -friendly→user-friendly relation, so retain untouched. Existing friend r_4222429765f091a7 and fri r_3b3cfb8759029490 share g_3c10c276ee206ded; historically related, without implying the combining form is merely bound or that fri is its modern segment.

entries.origin: English composite teaching suffix, analyzed as -ist plus -ics; historical word formation varies
entries.source_entry: -istics; College of San Mateo suffix examples
entries.reason: The exact listed common example statistics permits a stronger educational lookup than the previously reviewed linguistics example: statistics = stat + istics is the visible grouping in the suffix table, while modern statistics is the study of data rather than necessarily only of states. The table does not explicitly print stat + -istics or prove that contemporary English directly coined the whole word by adding an indivisible suffix. Collins records the suffix as a combination of -ist and -ics; preserve this layered structure and German/Latin history. If the intended standard requires a source explicitly printing both constituent strings, the table still does not meet that narrower requirement and this item should remain pending. -ics→statistics e_8ee0b8577ef6819e475c for s_be8e872f4b01d5ce8952 is accepted in imports/uncontested-979/ready/notes/batches/979-supported-additions.json. stat→statistics e_0276ac1d82bc1001d174 for s_42c95a35bfb509d58eea is accepted in imports/resolved-pending.json as German Statistik / Italian statista from Latin status with evolved modern sense. Preserve both; neither is a previous -istics edge.

entries.meaning: a female person associated with the indicated occupation
entries.origin: French feminine agent form, from adjectival Latin -osa by later analogy, used in French loans
entries.source_entry: -euse
entries.reason: Dictionary.com explicitly records -euse in French loans as forming feminine nouns corresponding to -eur; the exact complete word masseuse denotes a woman who gives massage. French morphology and the English loanword are evidence; do not assert that the English word was coined productively by English masse + -euse. Gender-specific masseuse can carry dated or inappropriate associations in professional settings; massage therapist is a useful register note. Collins describes Latin -osa as feminine of adjectival -osus and its later French extension by analogy: the Latin suffix itself should not be asserted to have meant a female agent. Existing -eur state sense is a different entry. No exact -euse→masseuse rejection located in the specified checked records; prior unrelated -eur sense remains unchanged.

entries.meaning: chosen for an office but not yet serving
entries.source_entry: -elect
entries.reason: Cambridge Business labels -elect a suffix with the required elected-but-not-yet-in-office sense, while the Virginia style manual labels it a suffix and supplies president-elect. Cambridge Academic and Collins analyze elect as a postpositive adjective, including the same sense. Record both analyses: class suffix is an explicitly sourced practical classification, not proof that it is exclusively bound. Keep the hyphen in this example. Cambridge content was verified through the search engine index; direct fetching returned 403. No exact -elect→president-elect exclusion located in checked records. Historical lect relations and existing distinct families are not automatically merged.

entries.meaning: having a specified kind or status of name
entries.origin: Greek name-related combining form, later used in English adjectives; historical and teaching analyses vary
entries.source_entry: -onymous
entries.reason: The exact final sequence -onymous is attested as a name-related combining form; sources analyze an-onymous and the word means a person or source whose name is unknown or withheld. The privative an- provides the negation: the complete word does not say that an identified name exists. Anonymous entered through Greek and Latin, so the breakdown is historical/analytical, not a claim it was newly coined in English by attaching -onymous. Affixes.org and World Wide Words share an author and do not constitute two independent sources; the Cambridge Grammar excerpt was checkable via search index but its large PDF could not be fetched by the browsing tool. A combining-form/base analysis is an alternative to class suffix; keep the qualification. Link to existing onym/nym family g_f5a594e2414a35bd rather than the privative prefix family. Preserve onym→anonymous accepted e_afdb71e22be779624003, sources s_1eff89029837142c00eb, s_848720dc8f9ee748e08f, s_b0f7927706ef5f17162c, s_e5c855c8875cd4ca78c1; a→anonymous accepted e_2362057666bc1dc53e5c and an→anonymous accepted e_dbcca9cc7c7a8309eb5e, source s_ad76a1f0173d23f66ffe. The a record is a related privative variant, not the visible an- spelling. None is an exclusion of this longer form.

entries.meaning: a catastrophic or supposedly catastrophic event involving the specified thing
entries.origin: English reanalysis from apocalypse; informal or playful use
entries.source_entry: -pocalypse
entries.reason: Linguistics study explicitly associates -(p)ocalypse with apocalypse and snowpocalypse; UPenn Language Log separately calls -pocalypse a libfix. Dictionary.com identifies snowpocalypse as a severe snowstorm or overreaction, and labels its page an informal slang summary.
